sections.text:
They argue further: even if we are baptized into the Spirit, that does not justify ranking him with God, because some “were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” Likewise Scripture can speak of faith in a human being: “The people believed God and Moses his servant.” Why then, they ask, do faith and baptism lead us to magnify the Holy Spirit above creation when similar expressions have been used of human beings?

We reply that faith in the Spirit is faith of the same order as faith in the Father and the Son, and the baptism likewise. But baptism into Moses and the cloud was into a shadow and a type.

Divine realities are often prefigured by small and human things, but the use of a humble type does not make the divine reality itself small. A type is an anticipatory representation of what is expected, showing beforehand by imitation what is to come. Adam was “a type of the One to come”; the rock was typologically Christ; the water from the rock signified the life-giving power of the Word: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” The manna prefigured the living bread that came down from heaven. The serpent raised on the standard prefigured the saving Passion accomplished through the cross, so that those who looked upon it were preserved.

In the same way the history of Israel's exodus was recorded as a sign of those saved through baptism. The firstborn of Israel were preserved, just as the bodies of the baptized are preserved, by grace given to those marked with blood. The lamb's blood was a type of Christ's blood, and the firstborn a type of the first-formed human nature. Because the first-formed Adam remains in us through the sequence of human generation, “in Adam all die,” and death reigned until the fulfillment of the law and the coming of Christ. The firstborn were preserved from the destroyer as a sign that those made alive in Christ no longer die in Adam.

The sea and the cloud produced faith at that time through wonder, but as types they also prefigured the grace to come. “Who is wise and will understand these things?” The sea typologically signifies baptism because it separates from Pharaoh just as this washing separates from the devil's tyranny. The sea destroyed the enemy within itself; in baptism our hostility toward God dies. The people came out of the sea unharmed; we too rise from the water as those alive from the dead, saved by the grace of the One who called us. The cloud is a shadow of the Spirit's gift, cooling the flame of the passions through the putting to death of our earthly members.

What then? Because they were baptized into Moses in a type, is the grace of baptism therefore small? If we judged every Christian reality by the lowliness of its Old Testament type, nothing belonging to us would remain great.

The love of God who gave his Only-begotten Son for our sins would cease to seem extraordinary merely because Abraham did not spare his son. The Passion of the Lord would cease to be glorious because a sheep was offered in place of Isaac as its type. The descent into Hades would cease to be awesome because Jonah prefigured death by spending three days and nights in the great fish.

The same mistake occurs when someone compares the reality of baptism with its shadow and uses Moses and the sea to depreciate the whole evangelical economy. What forgiveness of sins was there in the sea? What renewal of life? What spiritual gift came through Moses? What putting to death of sin took place there?

They did not die together with Christ; therefore they were not raised together with him. They did not bear the image of the heavenly One, did not carry the dying of Jesus in their body, did not put off the old human being, did not put on the new one renewed in knowledge according to the image of the Creator.

Why then compare baptisms that share only a name when the realities differ as much as a dream from reality, or shadow and image from the thing that exists in its own substance?

Nor does faith in Moses diminish faith in the Spirit. According to our opponents' reasoning it would rather diminish confession of the God of all, because Scripture says, “The people believed God and Moses his servant.” Moses is therefore joined in that sentence with God, not with the Spirit.

Moreover Moses was a type not of the Spirit but of Christ. In the ministry of the law he represented beforehand the Mediator between God and human beings. He mediated for the people in matters concerning God. The law was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator—namely Moses—in accordance with the people's request: “You speak to us, and let God not speak to us.”

Thus faith in Moses is referred to the Lord, the true Mediator between God and humanity, who said, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me.” Is faith in the Lord therefore small because it was signified beforehand through Moses? Certainly not. In the same way, even if people were baptized into Moses, the grace of the Spirit in Christian baptism is not thereby diminished.

Scripture also commonly uses “Moses” as a name for the law, as in: “They have Moses and the prophets.” So when Paul speaks of the baptism belonging to the law he says, “They were baptized into Moses.”

Why, then, do those who attack the truth use the shadow and the types to make contemptible the boast of our hope and the rich gift of our God and Savior, who through regeneration renews our youth like the eagle's?

It is childish to ignore the great mystery of salvation. In God's gradual pedagogy we are led toward perfection: at first through things easier to grasp and proportioned to our weakness, then toward the full light. The law has “a shadow of the good things to come,” and prophetic types are a dim presentation of truth, training the eyes of the heart so that the transition to wisdom hidden in mystery may become possible. Enough concerning types; otherwise the digression would become larger than the main argument.

translator_notes: Basil treats Moses, the sea, cloud, manna, rock, serpent, Isaac, and Jonah typologically rather than as realities equal to their New Covenant fulfillment.
The chapter distinguishes typological baptism 'into Moses' from sacramental baptism into Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
